summary: Specifies extensions to Kerberos, called PKINIT, that integrate public key cryptography into the initial authentication exchange. Users can authenticate using asymmetric signature or encryption algorithms in the pre-authentication data fields rather than only a password-derived key. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of telling a guard a secret word, you show a special ID card that only you could have. PKINIT lets Kerberos accept that kind of digital ID card at login.

subtitle: Lets a Kerberos client prove who it is with a certificate and private key instead of a password-derived key.

tldr.problem: In standard Kerberos the key that protects the initial reply is typically derived from the user's password, so the protocol is no stronger than the passwords people choose.
tldr.mechanism: The client signs its initial request with its private key and sends its certificate in a PA_PK_AS_REQ pre-authentication element. The KDC checks it and returns a signed PA_PK_AS_REP, delivering the reply key by Diffie-Hellman or by public key encryption.
tldr.outcome: After this one exchange the ticket-granting ticket works as usual, so everything later in Kerberos is independent of how the user first logged in. RFC 4556 is a Proposed Standard that has since been updated by RFC 6112, RFC 8062 and RFC 8636.

today: RFC 4556 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 6112, RFC 8062 and RFC 8636, so read it together with those. See RFC 6112, RFC 8062 and RFC 8636.

sections.title: Why Kerberos Needs Public Keys
sections.content:
Kerberos V5 (RFC 4120) uses a trusted third party, the Key Distribution Center (KDC), to hand out tickets. In the first step, the Authentication Service (AS) exchange, the client sends an AS-REQ and gets an AS-REP back. The reply is encrypted with the AS reply key, which for human users is typically derived from their password. The RFC points out the consequence: for human users, the attack resistance of Kerberos is no stronger than the strength of their passwords.

PKINIT replaces that one step. The client and the KDC each hold a public and private key pair and use them to authenticate each other and to agree on the AS reply key. The ticket-granting ticket is unchanged, so the client exposes its long-term secret only once, and all later authentication does not depend on how the initial login was done. The RFC lists further benefits: it fits existing public key infrastructure, and it spares users from managing strong passwords.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally your Kerberos login depends on a password, and a weak password makes the whole thing weak. PKINIT swaps the password for a digital ID card that is much harder to guess.

sections.title: How the Exchange Changes
sections.content:
PKINIT adds four things to the normal AS exchange. The client puts a special pre-authenticator in its initial request, holding its public-key data and a signature. The KDC tests the request against its authentication policy and its trusted Certification Authorities (CAs). If the request passes, the KDC replies as usual, except that the reply is encrypted with either a key from a Diffie-Hellman exchange or a symmetric key that is signed by the KDC and encrypted to the client's public key. Finally the client validates the KDC's signature, obtains the key, decrypts the reply and carries on as in RFC 4120.

Two new pre-authentication types carry this: PA_PK_AS_REQ (16) and PA_PK_AS_REP (17). PKINIT also defines a new authorization data type, AD_INITIAL_VERIFIED_CAS (9), and a set of new error codes. Everything is encoded with DER, and the RFC advises using DER for the Cryptographic Message Syntax objects too, since some implementations cannot decode indefinite-length BER.
sections.plainLanguage: The login still has a question and an answer. But the question is now signed with your private key, and the answer is locked so only you can open it.

sections.title: The Client Request
sections.content:
The AS-REQ carries a PA-PK-AS-REQ whose main field, signedAuthPack, holds a signed CMS object. Inside it is an AuthPack with four parts: a PKAuthenticator, an optional clientPublicValue (the client's Diffie-Hellman public value, present only if the client wants that method), an optional supportedCMSTypes list in decreasing preference, and an optional clientDHNonce used when DH keys may be reused.

The PKAuthenticator holds cusec and ctime for replay prevention, a random nonce, and a paChecksum, a SHA1 checksum over the KDC-REQ-BODY. The checksum field MUST be present. It is syntactically optional only so that a future client could drop SHA1; a KDC following this RFC answers such a request with KDC_ERR_PA_CHECKSUM_MUST_BE_INCLUDED.

The signed data also carries the client's certificates, enough to build a path to a trust anchor the KDC accepts, but never root CA certificates. The client may also list CAs it trusts in trustedCertifiers, and name a KDC key it already has in kdcPkId. When Diffie-Hellman is used, implementations MUST support Oakley 1024-bit MODP group 2 and 2048-bit MODP group 14, and SHOULD support 4096-bit MODP group 16.
sections.plainLanguage: The client writes its request, signs it, and staples its ID card to it. It also includes a quick fingerprint of the request so nobody can swap the contents.

sections.title: How the KDC Validates the Request
sections.content:
The KDC verifies the signature, validates the client's X.509 certificate and, depending on local policy, may check whether certificates on the path have been revoked. It must then check that the client's public key is bound to the principal name in the request. If the KDC has its own binding it uses that. Otherwise it looks for a Subject Alternative Name in the certificate carrying a KRB5PrincipalName under the id-pkinit-san identifier. No match produces KDC_ERR_CLIENT_NAME_MISMATCH.

The KDC MAY require the client certificate to carry the extended key usage id-pkinit-KPClientAuth, and SHOULD also accept the Microsoft smart card logon usage id-ms-kp-sc-logon as meeting that requirement. It must also check the timestamp for replay and clock skew, and check that any Diffie-Hellman parameters satisfy its policy. If they do not, it returns KDC_ERR_DH_KEY_PARAMETERS_NOT_ACCEPTED with a list of parameters it supports, from which the client SHOULD pick one to retry.

Each failure has its own error code, which lets a client tell whether to retry with other certificates or give up.
sections.plainLanguage: The KDC is the guard. It checks the signature, checks the ID card was issued by someone it trusts, and checks the card really belongs to the person named in the request.

sections.title: Delivering the Reply Key
sections.content:
If the request is valid, the KDC proceeds as in RFC 4120, sets the initial flag, and adds AD_INITIAL_VERIFIED_CAS authorization data to the ticket, naming the CAs on the path that validated the client. The AS-REP carries a PA-PK-AS-REP that selects one of two delivery methods. The ticket lifetime MUST NOT exceed the lifetime of the client's key pair.

Diffie-Hellman is the method every implementation MUST support. The KDC signs a KDCDHKeyInfo holding its DH public key and the request's nonce. Both sides compute the shared secret and turn it into the AS reply key with a function called octetstring2key, built from SHA1. A KDC that wants to reuse its DH keys must include an expiration time and a server nonce, and SHOULD NOT reuse keys unless the client sent a clientDHNonce.

Public key encryption is a SHOULD. The KDC generates the reply key, signs it together with a checksum of the AS-REQ inside a ReplyKeyPack, and encrypts the result to the client's public key. If the client did not offer DH and the KDC lacks this method, it returns KDC_ERR_PUBLIC_KEY_ENCRYPTION_NOT_SUPPORTED.
sections.plainLanguage: The KDC has to get a secret key to you without anyone else learning it. It can either agree on one with you by swapping clever numbers, or lock a fresh key in a box only your ID card can open.

sections.title: What the Client Checks
sections.content:
The client derives or decrypts the AS reply key, then verifies the KDC's signature and validates the KDC's X.509 certificate. Unless it can otherwise confirm that the signing key belongs to the KDC of the target realm, the certificate MUST carry a Subject Alternative Name with the id-pkinit-san type and a KRB5PrincipalName matching the realm's ticket-granting service. Unless the client knows by other means that the certificate is for a Kerberos KDC, it MUST also require the id-pkinit-KPKdc extended key usage. In the public key encryption case the client MUST verify the asChecksum, which ties the reply to its own request.

Only when all checks pass does the client decrypt the reply with the AS reply key and continue as in RFC 4120. The RFC also lets a KDC advertise PKINIT by listing an empty PA_PK_AS_REQ element in the error reply that asks for pre-authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: You check the guard too. Before trusting the reply, you make sure its signature is real and that the ID card really belongs to the right Kerberos server.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC stresses that the secret values, such as Diffie-Hellman exponents, must come from truly random bits. It also warns that Kerberos error messages are not integrity protected, so an attacker can tamper with the DH parameters a KDC suggests in a retry. Local policy can fix the acceptable parameter sets or disable negotiation.

PKINIT extends the cross-realm trust model to the public key infrastructure. A client MUST verify that the CA which issued a KDC certificate is authorized to issue KDC certificates for the target realm; otherwise the binding between certificate and KDC is not established. The RFC does not recommend using one RSA key pair for both encryption and signing, and notes that the DH method avoids this and avoids escrowed encryption keys.

PKINIT has no return routability test, so an attacker may try to make the KDC spend effort on public key operations. Reusing DH keys can reduce that cost per request. Finally, when DH is used, any additional pre-authentication data is not bound to the AS-REQ and could be dropped or added by an attacker unnoticed.
sections.plainLanguage: The lock is only as good as the randomness used to make it, and the system only works if you trust the right ID card makers. The RFC lists the places where that trust could go wrong.

messages.label: AS-REQ + PA_PK_AS_REQ
messages.note: Signed AuthPack, certificates, optional DH public value.

messages.label: KRB-ERROR
messages.note: Only if validation fails, for example KDC_ERR_CANT_VERIFY_CERTIFICATE.

messages.label: AS-REP + PA_PK_AS_REP
messages.note: Signed DH info or an encrypted key pack carrying the AS reply key.

items.label: KDC_ERR_CLIENT_NOT_TRUSTED
items.desc: Client public key not accepted for other reasons.

items.label: KDC_ERR_INVALID_SIG
items.desc: The client's signature failed to verify.

items.label: KDC_ERR_DH_KEY_PARAMETERS_NOT_ACCEPTED
items.desc: DH parameters fail KDC policy; supported ones are listed.

items.label: KDC_ERR_CANT_VERIFY_CERTIFICATE
items.desc: No certification path could be built.

items.label: KDC_ERR_REVOKED_CERTIFICATE
items.desc: A certificate on the path is revoked.

items.label: KDC_ERR_REVOCATION_STATUS_UNKNOWN
items.desc: Revocation status could not be determined.

items.label: KDC_ERR_CLIENT_NAME_MISMATCH
items.desc: Certificate is not bound to the requested client name.

items.label: KDC_ERR_INCONSISTENT_KEY_PURPOSE
items.desc: Required extended key usage is missing.

items.label: KDC_ERR_DIGEST_IN_CERT_NOT_ACCEPTED
items.desc: Digest used by a CA signature is not acceptable.

items.label: KDC_ERR_DIGEST_IN_SIGNED_DATA_NOT_ACCEPTED
items.desc: Digest used in the signed data is not acceptable.

items.label: KDC_ERR_PUBLIC_KEY_ENCRYPTION_NOT_SUPPORTED
items.desc: Client skipped DH and the KDC lacks public key encryption.
